description: Neptune's largest moon and one of the most geologically active worlds in the solar system. Triton orbits Neptune backwards (retrograde) and at an extreme tilt — diagnostic of a captured Kuiper Belt object, making it likely a sibling of Pluto rather than a native Neptunian moon. Voyager 2 detected active nitrogen geysers venting dark organic dust 8 km into a tenuous nitrogen atmosphere; the southern hemisphere features 'cantaloupe terrain' — a network of dimples and ridges seen nowhere else in the solar system. Triton's retrograde orbit is decaying tidally; in roughly 3.6 Gyr it will either be torn into a Saturn-like ring or crash into Neptune.
surface_composition: Frozen nitrogen + water ice + carbon dioxide ice; surface covered with cantaloupe-textured terrain unique in the solar system, and active nitrogen cryogeysers venting dark plumes 8 km into a thin nitrogen atmosphere.

science_sections.why: Triton's 156.8° orbital inclination — retrograde, steeply tilted to Neptune's equator — is the smoking-gun for capture from the Kuiper Belt rather than formation with Neptune.
Triton's tidal drag is decreasing its orbit — in 3.6 billion years it will either impact Neptune or fragment inside the Roche limit and form a ring system.
